editorialPolicy.storyFidelity: Each level preserves the complete event sequence, motivations, consequence, and chapter ending.
editorialPolicy.foundation: Concrete 6–11 word sentences, one main action per line, minimal subordinate clauses.
editorialPolicy.core: Connected 10–18 word sentences with cause, contrast, and reaction.
editorialPolicy.studio: Literary but speakable sentences that preserve narrator wit, suspense, and moral tension.
editorialPolicy.safety: Historic slapstick and peril are described without adding graphic detail. Harmful actions retain their consequences and are not presented as desirable.
editorialPolicy.narration: Dialogue is acted with restraint inside one continuous chapter-level performance; no independent sentence generations.

narration.direction: Open with generous relief, make the Fox smooth and persuasive and the Cat's repetition faintly comic, sharpen the Blackbird warning, and end with the uneasy confidence of a successful con.
narration.productionRule: Generate one continuous master per level and derive sentence timestamps from that same master.

livingStorybook.artBrief: A wide country-road panorama from the theater gate toward Geppetto's distant home: Pinocchio holds five gold pieces, a limping russet Fox and supposedly blind gray Cat flank him, a Blackbird warns from a fence, and an imagined golden tree glows like a tempting paper cutout on the horizon.

lines.text: Fire Eater gave Pinocchio five gold pieces.
The money was a gift for Geppetto.
On the road, Pinocchio met a Fox and Cat.
They pretended to be lame and blind.
A Blackbird warned Pinocchio not to listen.
The Fox promised a tree full of gold.
Pinocchio wanted to make his money grow.
He forgot Geppetto and followed the strangers.

lines.text: Fire Eater gave Pinocchio five gold pieces to carry home to Geppetto.
Pinocchio planned to buy his father a coat and replace the schoolbook.
Along the road, he met a limping Fox and a supposedly blind Cat.
The sight of the coins briefly made the Fox's paw and the Cat's eyes work.
A Blackbird warned Pinocchio that their advice would bring regret.
The Fox claimed that buried coins could grow into a tree of gold.
At first, Pinocchio refused because his father was waiting at home.
The Fox described thousands of coins and mocked the choice to study.
Greed made the impossible promise sound reasonable to the inexperienced puppet.
Forgetting his father and every good resolution, Pinocchio followed the pair.

lines.text: The next morning, Fire Eater learned of Geppetto's poverty and entrusted Pinocchio with five gold pieces for his father.
The delighted marionette set out planning both a warm coat for Geppetto and a new A-B-C book for himself.
Before he had traveled far, a limping Fox and a blind Cat greeted him with suspicious knowledge of his family.
The ring of gold momentarily restored the Fox's lame paw and opened the Cat's supposedly sightless eyes, though Pinocchio noticed neither clue.
A Blackbird delivered a direct warning, but the Cat silenced the honest voice and immediately resumed the performance of blindness.
The Fox then offered an effortless fortune: coins planted in the Field of Wonders would grow into a tree heavy with gold.
Pinocchio initially remembered Geppetto, the lost schoolbook, and the pain already caused by disobedience.
Yet the promise of thousands of coins transformed caution into calculation and greed into imagined generosity.
The Fox pretended to want nothing for himself, while the Cat echoed every lie as though repetition were proof.
Convinced that the swindlers were good people, Pinocchio turned away from home and placed himself in their hands.
